target_customer: People with opioid use disorder in the US, paying through insurance (including Medicaid) or cash
problem: Few doctors hold the waiver to prescribe buprenorphine, so people with opioid addiction struggle to get medication assisted treatment and often buy medication on the street.
business_model: Virtual clinic billing insurers and patients for telehealth visits and prescriptions

founders.name: Zack Gray
education: Wharton, University of Pennsylvania (graduate, per Daily Pennsylvanian headline)
founders.background_notes: Started the company after losing his girlfriend to an opioid overdose, per the company story page and YC page.

founders.name: Mattan Griffel
prior_employers: Columbia Business School (faculty, Innovation Fellow at the Lang Center)
education: New York University, philosophy and finance
previous_startups: An earlier YC-backed startup (name not given on the YC page)
founders.background_notes: YC page calls him a two-time YC-backed entrepreneur. The Daily Pennsylvanian headline names him as co-founder with Gray.

competitors.name: Bicycle Health
competitors.what: Exclusively virtual opioid use disorder treatment program

competitors.name: Eleanor Health
competitors.what: Virtual first addiction treatment peer named in a 2020 article

competitors.name: Halcyon Health
competitors.what: Virtual first addiction treatment peer named in a 2020 article

technical_complexity.rationale: Standard telehealth stack plus prescribing and compliance workflows; the hard parts were clinical operations and state licensing, not software.

defensibility.rationale: Licensing in many states and insurance contracts took time to build, but rivals launched the same virtual model in the same period.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent absorbed the wedge by 2024; the company expanded state by state and signed insurer and Medicaid contracts.

market_need_then: The YC page cites more than 3 million Americans addicted to opioids with 80 percent untreated, fewer than 5 percent of doctors holding the prescribing waiver, and telehealth flexibilities in 2020 that let virtual programs start.

branding.name_origin: Ophelia's own blog says Gray named it after Shakespeare's Ophelia, whose story embodies grief and loss, and because the name starts with the letters op like opioids. A 2021 Vator article adds a Greek etymology meaning help.
branding.domain_note: Company now uses ophelia.com; how it was acquired is not stated in sources found.

identity.visual_style: Soft consumer health look per the company site
identity.voice_and_tone: Hope not tragedy, no judgment, no stigma

branding.brand_signature: A founder story of loss told on the company blog, with the message that the story is one of hope
branding.community_and_virality: The company blog invites readers to share their own recovery stories under the Ophelia name; no merch or fan accounts found.

brand_strength.rationale: A memorable name and a strong founder story, but no evidence of viral or community driven growth.

outcome_analysis: Ophelia launched as telehealth rules loosened in 2020, grew to about 250 people and raised a 15 million dollar Series A in April 2021 and a 50 million dollar Series B in December 2021 from Tiger Global and others. It then added insurer and Medicaid contracts in New York and New Jersey. No layoffs, sale or shutdown turned up in searches, so it is treated as active and growing but with no later round found.
notes: A MobiHealthNews headline reports an earlier seed for Ophelia (written as 27m in the URL) but the page could not be opened, so no seed round is recorded. Total raised of about 68 million dollars is reported by search summaries of the Series B coverage. The Series A lead and investors rely on the BHBusiness and search summaries. Founding year is 2019 on the YC page and the Daily Pennsylvanian but some profiles say 2020.
